content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In Christian teaching, the coin most commonly functions as a symbol of image, ownership, and allegiance: because a coin bears the image and inscription of its issuer, it belongs to that issuer. In the dominant homiletic and patristic reading of the tribute-money episode ('render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's'), the coin stamped with Caesar's image represents what is owed to earthly authority, while the human being—stamped with God's image (Genesis 1:26-27)—belongs wholly to God. The coin thus symbolizes the question of ultimate ownership and where one's allegiance is due.","primary_basis":["Matthew 22:15-22","Mark 12:13-17","Luke 20:20-26","Genesis 1:26-27 (paired with the tribute-coin passage in patristic and modern preaching to argue that humans are God's 'coinage,' bearing His image)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"The lost coin as the lost sinner or lost soul: precious to God, diligently sought, and occasioning heavenly joy when recovered (Parable of the Lost Coin). Some patristic and medieval interpreters (e.g., Gregory the Great, Augustine) extended this to the coin as the image of God in the human soul, obscured by sin and recovered through grace.","basis":["Luke 15:8-10"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Thirty pieces of silver as the symbol of betrayal, treachery, and 'blood money'—the price at which Christ was valued and sold, often linked typologically to Zechariah's thirty shekels and to the price of a slave in Exodus.","basis":["Matthew 26:14-16","Matthew 27:3-10","Zechariah 11:12-13","Exodus 21:32"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The widow's two small coins (mites/lepta) as a symbol of sacrificial, wholehearted giving—true generosity measured by cost to the giver rather than by amount.","basis":["Mark 12:41-44","Luke 21:1-4"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The denarius in the parable of the laborers in the vineyard as a symbol of God's grace or the equal reward of eternal life, given without regard to human calculations of merit.","basis":["Matthew 20:1-16"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"The coin in the fish's mouth as a symbol of God's providential provision and/or Christ's freedom from the temple tax coupled with voluntary compliance to avoid offense.","basis":["Matthew 17:24-27"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Coins/money generally as a symbol of mammon—worldly wealth as a rival object of devotion opposed to God.","basis":["Matthew 6:24","Luke 16:13","1 Timothy 6:10"],"prominence":"common"}],"has_settled_consensus":false,"confidence":"medium","notes":"'Coin' does not carry a single fixed symbolic meaning in Christian interpretation; its significance is strongly context-dependent, varying across the tribute money, the lost coin, the thirty pieces of silver, the widow's mites, and the vineyard denarius. The most frequently taught and most theologically developed symbolism is the image-and-ownership reading of the tribute coin (humans bear God's image and therefore belong to God), which has deep patristic roots (e.g., Tertullian, Augustine) and remains standard in modern preaching, so it is listed as primary. However, the lost-coin and thirty-silver-pieces readings are nearly as widely recognized in their own contexts. Any author claiming one exclusive, settled symbolic meaning for 'coin' across Scripture would be going beyond recognizable consensus."}
